opening: Lord, meet us gently today and always
body:
Does Jesus heal the wicked?
Yes—but only the wicked who are willing to become sinners in need of mercy.
Jesus healed tax collectors, adulterers, thieves, persecutors, and eventually even Saul, who became Paul. None of them healed themselves. They allowed themselves to be found.

The truly dangerous heart is not the sinful one; it is the one that says, "I have nothing to repent of." 

How can one person inflict harm on another?
God created human beings capable of genuine love. But genuine love requires genuine freedom. That same freedom can be twisted into selfishness, hatred, pride, and violence. If God removed our ability to choose evil, He would also remove our ability to choose love.  That doesn't make the suffering any less heartbreaking. The Bible never minimizes it. It laments it over and over.

What the readings today reveal together is this progression:
Wickedness is real.
The vulnerable are not invisible to God.
God's justice may seem delayed, but it is coming.
Jesus extends hope beyond every boundary—to Jew and Gentile, victim and sinner alike.
The invitation to healing is open, but it must be received.
One thought does stand out: "The vulnerable feel unfortunate, but the Lord sees."
That may be the center of today's readings. Evil often makes people feel unseen and forgotten. God answers, not first with immediate punishment of the wicked, but by saying, "I see you." The cross becomes the ultimate proof of that. God did not remain distant from human cruelty; He entered into it, suffered it, and overcame it. Justice and mercy meet there. The wicked are offered repentance, the wounded are offered hope, and both are invited into the same Kingdom.
